subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 12, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-243, to amend the National Defence Act and other acts in consequence thereof-Mr. Hellyer-Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Order. When the committee rose last evening clause 2 was under consideration.
April 13, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment
On clause 2-Canadian forces, Canadian armed forces.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it had not been my purpose to take part in this discussion, but in spite of the fact that I do not pretend to be a defence expert, and as a matter of fact have little experience with regard to matters connected with the defence department, I am impelled to take part in the discussion because I believe the emphasis in this debate as outlined by the Minister of National Defence, by his cabinet colleagues and by his supporters has not been constructive but rather destructive. All these gentlemen appear determined to pursue a course which I am convinced is in most respects detrimental to the defence of Canada in present day conditions, either when carried out in co-operation with our allies or by ourselves, and in the fulfilment of our world wide commitments.
First of all I should like to remind the house of the importance of what we are doing here. The fact that we have before us a bill which drastically amends the National Defence Act seems to me to justify very careful examination of this point. Before we even contemplate such a drastic change should we not satisfy ourselves that it is needed?
Before we consider whether the bill before us constitutes an improvement I think we should look over the record of the last half century. We will find, of course, that from a defence point of view we have participated in two world wars. It is my opinion, it has always been my opinion and I believe it will continue to be my opinion, that the world wide prestige of Canada and the glorious reputation which our country has earned for itself is mostly due to our participation in two world wars and to the fact that our servicemen have risen to every occasion and have covered themselves and Canada with glory. Surely I do not need to remind the house that within the last few days our Associate Minister of National Defence made a pilgrimage to the scene of the battle at Vimy, where history was made and a glorious tradition established for us, for our country and for our children to view with pride, a tradition which has gone down in the annuals of our nation.
This is part of the record I am asking members of the house to examine. I ask also that the price paid be remembered. Many Canadian lives were lost, many Canadian bodies were broken and many Canadians were crippled for life. So let us not tamper lightly
[The Chairman.]
with the National Defence Act under which these men fought our country's battles.
I will proceed to an examination of the record. Now I come to world war II. I remind the house of the six year period during which the Canadian forces were engaged in many areas of conflict. I remind them of the battle of Britain, of the campaigns in Italy and North Africa, the Dieppe raid and the invasion of France. I pay full tribute to the many people within sound of my voice this afternoon who fought in these battles. Men from all sides and all quarters of this house participated.
It seems to me that before any drastic change-and I emphasize "drastic change" once more-is made in the act this house should carefully examine the record and preserve all that has stood the test of time for more than half a century, during which two world wars were fought and the freedom of the world was at stake. I ask the house, is it not sensible and logical to preserve everything in the present act which has stood the test not only of time but of wartime? Then, Mr. Chairman, having done this, we can strengthen the act in the light of the changed conditions of today.
I agree that we must keep our National Defence Act up to date in the light of the changed conditions of 1967 compared with those of 20 years ago. Having examined the record and decided that we need to reassess and improve the act, let us see what the minister and the government are recommending to the representatives of the people, who after all have the final decision to make. At this point let us keep in mind one fact, and I ask the minister to particularly take note of it. Changes should be made only in the best interest of the defence of Canada and the people of Canada.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: That will be done.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
I for one am not satisfied that every clause in this bill presently under discussion does fall within that qualification. Let us examine the title of this act, Mr. Chairman. Bill No. C-243 is an act to amend the National Defence Act and other acts in consequence thereof. The short title is the Canadian Forces Reorganization Act. Sections 15 to 18 of the National Defence Act are repealed, and I should like at this point to
April 13, 19G7	COMMONS
refer to what section 15 of the old act says. It reads as follows:
The Canadian forces are the naval, array and air forces of Her Majesty raised by Canada and consist of three services, namely, the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force.
The new act substitutes the following:
The Canadian forces are the armed forces of Her Majesty raised by Canada and consist of one service called the Canadian Armed Forces.
What does this new provision do, Mr. Chairman? Chiefly it drops the word "royal."
I would ask why that word is dropped? Does dropping the word improve the forces or the ability of the forces to defend Canada? This is one point on which 1 should like the minister to make a statement and explain that omission.
I should like the members of the committee to examine the meaning of the word "royal." Webster's dictionary states that it means magnificent, majestic, excellent. It also says it pertains to a king. In simple language, Mr. Chairman, it implies that this is the superlative of excellence. Why do we drop the word if it denotes the superlative of excellence? If I had my way I would leave it in. If the government's supporters would vote for it I would propose an amendment that the new force be called the "royal Canadian armed forces."
In addition to changing the name, Mr. Chairman, what does the bill presently under consideration contemplate? As I recall the minister's speech, he advanced the idea that when he assumed his responsibilities as minister of defence some four years ago he decided that three things had to be undertaken. The first was to bring the past up to the present, by which he meant we should acquire nuclear warheads for the weapons systems. The second task was to review the equipment programs outstanding; the third was to determine a long range defence policy for Canada.
This was all in progress long before he became minister; there is no question of that. In the result, Mr. Chairman, we acquired nuclear weapons. The minister stated that it was the unanimous opinion of the chiefs of staff and the staff members-and I hope and pray, as I am sure we all do, that this assumption is correct-that a nuclear war was the least likely. The minister has informed us that we are protected, to the extent that we can be protected, against a surprise nuclear attack. Therefore this disposes of that particular requirement.
National Defence Act Amendment
The minister mentioned the need for flexibility and mobility. As a layman I find no fault with this. I suggest this would mean we should acquire more planes and ships. We are all faced with the need for more flexibility in our respective businesses.
The minister also mentioned the absence of an over-all strategic plan applied to the three services. He deplored lack of co-ordination of equipment programs for the determination of priorities from a national point of view. I do not believe there is very much difference of opinion on this question. The question of national priorities is pretty well understood and agreed with, I suggest. The minister then stressed the need for co-operation to fulfil objectives. There seems nothing wrong with this. He emphasized the need for equipment purchase priorities with national defence in mind.
The conclusion to all these proposals, Mr. Chairman, was of course integration and integrated action; and the minister has outlined the steps which were taken. I emphasize here that there has been little if any objection to the broad principle of integration, though I am sure all of us in this house will agree that it is quite a gigantic task to undertake.
The minister has mentioned the formation of one intelligence agency to replace five. He has mentioned a 30 per cent reduction in personnel in this branch, which he suggests means a financial saving. He has referred to construction engineering and to the advantage of applying common knowledge and experience, again suggesting there will be a saving. There is no objection to this; it is one facet of integration. The minister has also given some information relative to recruitment, and there is no objection to this. He also mentioned information services which have reduced expenditures.
The minister made specific reference to NORAD and air defence command. He forecast a saving of 30 per cent. He mentioned communications, and stated that a long line system for the Canadian armed forces will result in a saving of 18 per cent. The minister stated that the new system is working very satisfactorily. Most of all, he said, it is enabling the defence department to have studies made.
The minister referred to the new combined cataloguing system and the saving in personnel which would result in a 26 per cent financial saving. The minister suggested that all
April 13, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment these savings will mean great financial advantage so far as defence spending is concerned.
Adding all these percentages together, Mr. Chairman, it would appear that the minister expects large savings in defence expenditures. Now, Mr. Chairman, what are the facts? The facts simply are these, that in the estimates tabled in this house a few weeks ago the sums allocated to defence have increased over last year by $115 million, and this after the minister has told us of percentage savings on this item, that item and the other item.
The minister's remarks relative to equipment are to be remembered, Mr. Chairman. I do not propose to repeat them, but he did bring together integration and unification in this regard, and this is what I take objection to. I cannot agree with the unification principle, the doing away with branches of the armed forces and with famous regiments. Integration has been under way for some years and generally speaking it is not unacceptable, but I suggest to the minister unification is an altogether different question.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
It is for the minister to show that the bill we are presently studying will improve the ability of the people of Canada to provide for their own defence. I suggest that the minister has not done so. This is not only my opinion but the opinion of many senior officials in his own department, or at least they were members of his department. The minister glibly implies that they are fuddy-duddies who do not care to lose their privileges. I prefer to take the opinion of the career people who have served the country in war and in peace with great distinction rather than the opinion of the minister who seems to wish to disregard his closest and most able advisers if their advice conflicts with the preconceived notions he has acquired through his limited experience in the performance of his duties.
The question on which we are to vote is: Are the suggested changes good for Canada? Will they effect an improvement in the light of modern advancement? I submit the answer is no and I propose to prove that.
Before the minister concluded his remarks on Monday, April 3, he said he would deal with some of the myths which had been raised. This is where he and I part company so far as agreement is concerned. He delves into the world of the theoretical in his reference to so-called myths. He goes up into the


clouds. He says the uniforms of the servicemen make little difference, and that the question has been effectively answered. I say, I do not know when, or by whom. He says that uniforms are not unimportant. I say they are very important.
I now digress for a moment. I wish to make my position perfectly clear. The minister simply has not proven his case for unification. That is what he should do. It is not our responsibility to prove he is wrong; it is his responsibility to prove he is right.
No minister of any government should tamper with the defence of the country and make forays into the unknown, all in one big jump. Governments should be satisfied to make necessary changes step by step, one at a time, creeping before they walk, experimenting slowly and bewaring of blundering. We cannot afford to blunder when the defence of our country is at stake. This government has an unenviable record for blundering.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
That is the question for the Prime Minister to answer. Will the suggested changes improve the ability of our defence department to defend the people of Canada properly? The judgment of many senior officers, generals, admirals, air vice-marshals, distinguished in war and peace is no, they will not. The Minister of National Defence, with practically no experience, says yes, they will. The Prime Minister must decide. I appeal to him to make the good, the well-being of the people of Canada the paramount consideration and to let nothing else matter because the good of Canada should override every other consideration.
I return to my comments regarding Bill No. C-243. The members of this committee have a solemn responsibility when they vote. They must be satisfied that what they vote for is in the best interest of Canada and the defence of Canada. Defence has been referred to by Webster as meaning "resistance to and protection from attack". I repeat those words, "resistance to and protection from attack".
The question we all ask ourselves is whether the changes contemplated will strengthen the ability of our defence forces to resist and protect the country from attack. Many opinions have been expressed. Let us submit them to critical examination and then record our opinion by voting. The government have submitted Bill C-243 which does not stand up under critical examination on the basis that it will effect an improvement over the existing
April 13, 1967

act. It appears to me that they are again guilty of a tampering which will prove to be blundering. I do not believe that the armed forces can be organized for unification in a hurry. I believe it is possible to effect the improvements of integration and still retain the distinguishing and distinguished units, of which there are many, in which many hon. members within sound of my voice have served.
While we acknowledge that equipment and machines play an ever-increasing part in defence, I do not think we can ignore the individual and the part he plays in defence operations. Those advocating changes in the National Defence Act should have in mind the general desirability of appealing to the young men of our country to make a career of the defence of our country. To appeal to young people and to keep recruiting and enlistment on a proper basis it is necessary that young men be able to select the service of their choice and wear a uniform indicating the particular service in which they choose to serve. It is an elementary part of freedom that people select their vocations in life. In the free world we emphasize the right of young men and women to select their lifetime occupations. The record of productivity in the United States and Canada illustrates the wisdom of this feature of our social and economic life.
Where the uniforms of sailors, airmen and soldiers are of the same colour, material and design it is difficult to distinguish one branch of the forces from another, and this will discourage recruiting. Some young men will lose interest in joining. Most young people have natural aptitudes and work best at what they like to do. This bill makes little appeal to our young people to use their talents in the service of their choice and may prevent them from making the maximum contribution toward their own happiness. The bill should make a career in the armed services attractive and it does not do so. It should provide for the saving of money on certain things and it has not done so. It has been said that a certain percentage of money will be saved but according to documents tabled expenditures on defence show an increase of over $100 million over last year's figure.
This bill ought to be so drafted that it will improve the efficiency of the defence forces. The minister says it will do that but many senior officials say it will not. Many senior officers appeared before the standing committee during its 50-odd meetings. Many, with
National Defence Act Amendment long experience and knowledge respecting military matters, said that this measure will not increase efficiency and will not effect an improvement. That was the opinion of distinguished soldiers, sailors and airmen who fought in the war, who have served their country in peace and war. They deserve better than to have reflections cast on them by anyone. I have more confidence in the judgment of these experienced senior officers than I have in that of the minister at the present time.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
To summarize, I have made the point I wished to make. I have said I do not feel that the National Defence Act should be tampered with unless an improvement will result. This bill will not have that effect. Remember, we in this committee are tampering with the defence of Canada, something which does not deserve to be treated lightly. I submit that many portions of the bill are premature, ill-conceived and ill-considered. The measure should not be supported in its entirety. It will not improve the ability of the defence department to perform its proper function, the defence of Canada.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, new ideas are not easily come by nor do they develop overnight. New ideas are not put into practice easily because invariably they conflict with traditions and with customs. In the circumstances surrounding the issue before us there is ample opportunity to discuss the theory of change, social and political conflict, and the moulding of new practice.
For some time now we have been in the thick of this debate on the unification of the armed forces of Canada. It is gratifying to me to travel around my riding and hear people express their opinions on the unification issue. There is a great desire to see us get on with the passage of the bill because, as many people have stated to me, there has been enough discussion, enough repetition. It is now time for a final decision to be made and for consequent action to follow.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
I do not profess to be a military expert, nor do I pretend to be a pessimist about change. As I am not a military expert it is not my intention to discuss all the technicalities that are more familiar to military minds. I feel, however, that there are many

First, I want to say something concerning the young people of Canada. The tasks performed by our service personnel are complex and specialized. I found that the tried and true channels of communication which had been the warp and woof of navy, army and air force procedures in chain of command for decades had largely been discarded. I found that officers working for me knew more, or said they knew more, or thought they knew more, about what was in the mind of the minister than I did. subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, originally, like many others, I had no intention of entering the debate on Bill C-243. I felt justifiably that the members of the defence committee, at least those on this side of the house, were infinitely more qualified than I to discuss the intricacies of the evidence on this most important matter. I believe my confidence in my colleagues has been confirmed and strengthened by the excellent speeches they have made. As I perused the monumental work of the defence committee I was proud of the exemplary way in which they discharged their duties as Her Majesty's loyal opposition.
What has dismayed me, however, is the epidemic of intransigence that has afflicted the government side. Incidentally, I make no apology for medical references. Indeed, they seem to have become an integral part of this

debate. I recall hearing some reference to obstetrical measures by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra who referred to cutting the umbilical cord after a baby is born. This is astounding because presumably the baby would still be in utero. The epidemic seems to have been spread by the minister to almost every member on the government side. One might well ask what the symptoms of this affliction are. I shall delineate them, but first may I hazard a guess that the epidemic started from a germ of an idea which was somehow fully incubated in the laboratory of perhaps an executive assistant. I think it started in that way and has been spread by the minister.
The symptoms of this affliction are, as will become obvious, all mental, and the first is confusion. In this regard one has only to read the words of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra to understand how confusion has become one of the symptoms. The second is vertigo, a medical term which perhaps I had better explain. It means dizziness, going around in circles. We can all recognize immediately that this has been epitomized by the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The third is incoherence. Who else but the Minister of Transport? Fourth, and above all, is intransigence.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
What I simply cannot understand is how the government can be so uncompromising in face of the clarity and cogency of the arguments presented by the opposition. Why does the minister have to be contumacious instead of conciliatory? Why is he not sage instead of so stubborn? Surely the words of the military experts before the defence committee have meant something. Surely their years of experience count to a certain degree. Can we simply dismiss their views in a cavalier manner as being hopelessly out of date or are they just out of step with the minister, 'out of step with our Charlie?'
How in heaven's name can the expertise which has been exhibited by so many of the best brains of the armed forces of our country be completely ignored and tossed aside as completely unimportant? Yes, we have heard the evidence. On looking over the evidence one finds that there seems to be a preponderance in favour of delaying the bill, until integration is complete and working well, which from the evidence apparently it is not, until we have a chance to reassess what unification really means, and until we have a chance to plan a proper foreign policy and a proper utilization of the Canadian armed forces in
April 13. 1967	COMMONS
the framework of such a proper foreign policy. It is inconceivable to me that the words of Canada's foremost experts can be dealt with so cavalierly. I believe their words bear repetition.
But first, what are the real issues before the house and the country today? Surely one of the issues is morale. Another is the savings that may be effected by the proposed unification. Increased efficiency is another. Another is the matter of conscription. Another is, exactly what do we mean by unification? Another is incompatibility with foreign armed services and, most important of all, our ability to meet our commitments with a unified force.
If we turn to the evidence we find that the question of morale was dealt with by the experts who appeared before the committee. I have heard many comments from hon. members on the other side of the house that morale in the forces is fine. As one reads the speeches one finds the minister saying that morale is at an all-time high. The minister is shaking his head. I happen to agree with that shake of the head. Then we listen to hon. members on this side of the house and hear that morale is seriously affected. But when it is discovered that morale is not as good as it was, hon. members on the other side of the house blame us and say we are responsible for it because we are doing our job as a loyal opposition in the House of Commons.
Air Marshal Annis made a comment on morale which is to be found on page 1435 of the proceedings of the committee on national defence. I will not read it all but in part it reads as follows:
Therefore it is the worry about the morale and the difficulty of acquiring into the services and retaining the hard core people that I worry about. Unification, in my opinion, would have a very difficult psychological impact on them.
He goes on to say that we should have more time, which is a point that has been raised many times in the house. If I may paraphrase his remarks, he points out that unless we have time to see what this program is going to do and to plan properly, the detrimental effect on morale may be incalculable. The last part of his statement in this regard reads this way:
It might even happen that the time would come when we could safely say, "We are going to unify", and a gasp of dismay through these trades would just not occur.
It might, but we must have time to look carefully at this matter and try to understand what the minister is proposing. General
National Defence Act Amendment Foulkes, as found on page 1216 of the committee proceedings, said:
Another issue which has come in for a lot of criticism has been the lack of authentic information. Information was replaced by rumour and conjecture, which no doubt disturbed the morale of the forces.
I will leave out a few sentences. Then he said:
This, Mr. Chairman, in my view, is the surest way of breaking down the morale of any force.
In other words, lack of information. All that we on this side of the house have been trying to get is information from the minister. But he has built around himself an ivory tower in which he is unassailable and unavailable so far as clarification is concerned. The minister makes a great many comments. I have heard most of them. He made quite a speech the other day about what was going on in the United States. What this had to do with unification I did not quite understand.
General Foulkes in his testimony quoted General Montgomery, Monty, as he was known. At page 1217 of the committee proceedings, referring to Monty's memoirs he said:
He can think, he can appreciate, and he is definitely prepared to criticize.
He was talking about the fighting soldier. The passage continues:
He wants to know what is going on, and what you want him to do, and why and when. He wants to know, in doing it, that his best interests will be absolutely secure in your hands.
General Foulkes went on to say:
Mr. Chairman, I strongly urge that those responsible for implementing unification ponder over these remarks, especially over the last sentence-
Then he repeats it:
He want to know, in doing it, that his best interests will be absolutely secure in your hands.
Unless he has the information and knows what is going to happen the inevitable result, as is already happening and as we have seen from the minister's acquiescence, is that morale will decline. Morale is beginning to suffer. General Moncel also commented on morale. At page 1308 of the minutes of the proceedings of the committee the hon. member for York-Sunbury asked this question:
How much value, General Moncel, do you put on morale and esprit de corps in private units and private service in the matter of ability and willingness to do a job in this disturbed world?

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
It obviously is a very, very real factor. In a voluntary force such as ours it is of very real importance.

National Defence Act Amendment
So there is no question that morale has suffered. There is no question either, if we had proceeded with integration with which we all agree and this red herring had not been brought in, this idea that was conceived for what purpose no one knows, although there have been many suggestions, to unify our forces and put them all into one basket, what would have happened to morale. Surely not what has happened. The minister has talked about the tremendous savings that unifying the forces will mean for the Canadian taxpayer. The hon. member for Northumberland has already pointed out that these "savings" have already amounted to an additional expense of $161 million to the Canadian taxpayer. If these are savings I would very much hate to see what would happen when we tried to increase expenses.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I go now to page 1452 of the proceedings and evidence of the committee where the following question and answer appear:

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: Do you see any advantage in doing away with our present three forces and putting them into one force called just a defence force?

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Not the slightest hit; it baffles me completely. I think the economies could be achieved by much more simple means and I do not understand the advantages of this proposal at all.
Again, at page 1476, in answer to a question put to him by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, Mr. Hendrick said:
No, I cannot. From the details, as they appear to me, now outside the service, I cannot see anything that would cause a saving. As I said earlier, I do not even believe the savings are substantial in eliminating waste. I believe the only way you can save money in substantial amount is to cut the manpower. That really is the only basic way you can save money in substantial quantities.
That was the answer given by an expert. The minister has done even better than that. He has cut the manpower and raised the expenses. I wonder what some economists would have to say about this new approach to saving?
On the matter of economies General Moncel pointed out at page 1335 of the committee evidence that it would cost much more money to operate with a unified force in conjunction with our allies. I quote the following excerpt from that page:

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: In effect, in order to produce any reasonable defence effort commensurate with our population, our manufacturing ability and our general economic situation, we have to operate with allies.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Yes, unless you want to spend a great deal more money.

Yet the minister says we are going to save money. At page 1330 of the committee proceedings, when General Moncel said there was no economy in unification the following exchange took place:

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: And I say it does not matter whether you call them by those names or not, in effect, you still have to have those three services.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
This is right, and there is no payoff for calling them anything else.
What about efficiency? We have heard how efficient the unified services are going to be. Let us say we unified parliament into one group under a prime minister. Would it not be tremendous? The government, which would be composed of everyone in the house, would bring in bills and they would be passed. The rights of the people of course and of those directly involved would be trampled upon. I ask hon. members to look at some of those countries where this has happened. It would be a very efficient parliament. We could even get home for very long summer vacations. We could get home for long Christmas and Easter vacations if we were still observing our religious traditions.
Let us turn now to page 1428 where Air Marshal Annis was giving evidence. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre asked the following question:

speechtext:
Do you see an increase in the fighting efficiency of the armed forces through unification?
Air Marshal Annis answered:
No, I do not, sir.
How definite can one be? Then he went on to say:
I do not see a great deal provided one is successful with integrating fully the supporting services and the top command structure.
Earlier I mentioned conscription. Surely that is what unification is. Members who are now in the armed services may or may not want to go into the unified service proposed by the minister but they are in effect being conscripted into the new force. I do not understand how the splinter parties at the far end on this side of the house can support conscription when they have opposed it in the House of Commons for so many years. The government is conscripting these men into the new force against their will.
What is unification? The minister's definition of unification is a dandy one. He says that unification is the end objective of a logical and evolutionary progression. One could

almost apply that to the evolution of the species. It would look pretty silly if every one of us looked like the Minister of National Defence.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: And what if we thought like him?

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE

I do not even want to think of going that far. It is much more than my mind could possibly stand at this late hour.
I wonder whether the experts who appeared before the committee really understood unification. At page 1233 of the committee proceedings the following exchange took place:

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE

It is completely beyond me.
Yet I have heard suggestions from hon. members on the other side of the house, including the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, that we on this side also lacked understanding. subtopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. S-31, respecting Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company-Mr. Blouin-Mr. Batten in the chair.
On clause 1-Extension of time for completion of line.

subtopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was present in the standing committee when this bill was discussed and I am surprised to find that the evidence taken before the committee is not yet available to us. Therefore there is some reluctance in discussing the bill at this time. The discussions in which I participated led me to believe that the extension of time for the completion of this railway is not necessarily in the interest of the community it will serve in view of the fact that the company has failed to live up to its original obligation.
Originally the Labrador Mining Company, which was owned and operated mainly by Hollinger Gold Mines, was granted a charter to build a railway line to bring out iron ore from the area in which it intended to operate. Many people have been inclined to wonder why the company sought a federal rather than a provincial charter, but a perusal of the map which has been supplied indicates that the line crosses the boundary between Quebec and Labrador at least once. I believe there are other spurs which cross the border, and for this reason a federal charter was sought.
In granting a charter to a company engaged mainly in mining one must bear in mind two major considerations. One is the advantage which will flow to the country in general by the opening up of a particular mining development. The second consideration is the service which will be provided to the people who will move into the area and become permanent residents. Obviously colonization takes place when a primary industry is developed in a given area and a community is built around that industry.
This company originally thought it would be able to use one of the ports in the northern extremity of the province of Quebec, namely,

April 13, 1967
Private Bills
Ungava Bay, as a terminal and loading point. I have been quite closely connected with the mining industry and I remember the discussions that took place about the deep sea transportation which would be available when this railway line was built to Ungava.
It seems to me that since May 14, 1947, when the charter was first granted, the situation has changed substantially. I think that the development contemplated at that time has been brought to pass. The communities of Schefferville, Labrador City, Wabush and other small settlements in the area have established themselves and mining activities have spread to the extent that several mining companies are now in operation. Throughout the whole area extensive developments are taking place and an immense number of strikes involving various minerals have been recorded. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in my opinion it is now doubtful that this company should be operating a railway at all as a directly and totally owned subsidiary. I wonder whether the time has now come when the major railway companies of Canada should establish connections to this area and provide the transportation facilities required.
Several years ago this company experienced considerable difficulty with Wabash iron mines. The company wished to start developing its own mine but found itself what the members of the transportation committee would call a captive shipper of the line in that it would have to meet the rates set by the line. As I say, a great deal of difficulty arose in providing the extension necessary to tap the ore bodies of the area. For this reason there was considerable consternation in the area which resulted in a number of hearings before the Board of Transport Commissioners. Eventually a second subsidiary railway not connected with the first was built, and this line is now tied into that development.
In the original act passed in 1947 section 19 reads as follows:
The Company may, within five years after the passing of this Act, commence to construct the line of railway, and may within ten years after the passing of this Act complete the said line of railway, and if within the said periods respectively the said line of railway is not commenced or is not completed and put in operation, the power of construction conferred upon the Company by the Parliament of Canada shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the said line of railway as then remains uncompleted.
In my opinion this is what should have happened, and it would have happened but for the extension granted by parliament in 1956 of an additional ten years, extending the

charter to 1967. The company is now returning to parliament, having done no further work on the line and given no further consideration to the problem, and asking for another extension of ten years to construct the line which has already been approved by parliament. The plans for the construction of the line have been submitted to agencies of the government and have met with the approval of parliament. Yet the line is no closer to completion than it was ten years ago. In their evidence before the committee officials of the company indicated, I suggest, that they had no intention whatever in the foreseeable future of extending the line to its final destination at Ungava Bay.
For this reason, I think this company is being both unfair and unreasonable in expecting parliament to extend its charter, which also gives it the right to limit the activity of other companies. The Board of Transport Commissioners would have to examine, of course, any additional request for railway facilities in the area, whether for the purpose of transporting ore from the mine or for the general conveyance of passengers. The board would have to consider the fact that a charter covering this area had already been granted.
It seems to me that the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company has been given a grave responsibility by parliament. In turn it has received a very large concession. It has been given the benefits of the Railway Act which allow it to conduct the business of railway transportation in all its forms -passenger service, baggage, movement of iron ore and minerals and other goods. It has been given the right to build hotels, telegraph and telephone lines, to operate pipe lines, to engage in shipping and in the development of all facilities made possible under Canadian railway legislation. In the minds of members of parliament when granting the original charter was the idea that in return for benefits the company would incur liabilities or obligations.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
The people living in the Ungava, Labrador and northern Quebec areas have the right to expect the railway company we are considering to provide a service so that agricultural, forest and other products may be shipped and the mining communities, as well as persons engaging in exploration, may have the benefit of rail transportation. It seems evident, however, that this company does not intend to continue the development desired. It asks
April 13, 1967

permission to extend its line for another 60 miles to join another line servicing another property. Though this company has come to parliament asking for an extension of time there is no legitimate reason for parliament to give a blank cheque, a charter to develop something that the company has no intention of developing. It seems that the company will do only a small portion of what it originally committed itself to do. I should like to see the railway extended to Ungava Bay and the Atlantic ocean. I should like to see railway lines extended in the northern areas of James Bay and Hudson Bay. We have many resources there. Enough iron ore exists in the Belcher Islands area to justify a railway being built on the east shore of Hudson Bay to provide service for a big steel plant which could be erected there.
Living in the north I am aware of the resources there. Communities will spring up around these resources and in time the entire area will be developed. I say that the Canadian National should have been entrusted with building a line to this northern area in Quebec. It was foolish to entrust a private company with the building of a railway to transport an important part of our natural resources. What has happened disturbs me.
The Labrador Iron Company can transport what it needs to transport much more easily than others who have no ownership in this railway. Parliament gave this company an important asset to help it develop its properties in the north. Some development has taken place and transportation needs for the area will continue to grow. Quite obviously, however, difficulties will arise should this line be extended to the Ungava area. Those difficulties were originally mentioned when the charter was first sought.
The management of Hollinger Mines has never been completely stupid. It was aware that Hudson strait freezes over, and that Ungava Bay is closed for many months of the year. It was aware of the difficulties of building a line into that area. Nevertheless the management did agree when seeking a charter to undertake development beyond its needs at that time. In fact, 150 to 200 miles north of where the line was to end large bodies of ore were blocked out.
I repeat that much development will take place in these northern areas. The hon. member representing the area in question is optimistic about its future. Having connections with diamond drilling companies working in that area, I am familiar with the fact that 23033-9411

there is a tremendous potential for mining minerals there. It is estimated that there are hundreds of millions of tons of various kinds of ore there. I maintain that companies wishing to develop that region will have to depend for another ten years, should this charter be granted, on a company that may not build the railway that is needed.
Is it the intention of parliament to let this entire northern area be at the mercy of a company that may not build a needed railway? Do we in this house not wish to provide transportation facilities for the northern mining areas? Do we not wish to see transportation needs and rates determined by the Board of Transport Commissioners rather than by a private company? The board could set rates based on the cost of operating that railway. I point out that this private company would not be responsible to the board. Users of the railway would not have the board's protection.
I represent an area serviced by a provincial railway which operates in a manner different from that of other railways. It is interesting to note, for instance, that the Ontario Northland Railway employs licensed engineers, though other similar companies do not insist on their engineers having licences. Department of Transport examinations are the only criteria required.
It is also interesting to note that iron pellets are transported to Pittsburgh via five lines at a cost of less than $100 per car. I am told that the clay necessary for making these pellets comes from Manitoba over two lines at a cost of $285 per car. As can be seen, there is a great difference if goods are coming into the area or are being taken from it. I cite this example to show that the people in northern Labrador will find themselves in a similar situation.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
There is a great disparity between the needs of the people and those of industry in that area. You subsidize one and you soak the other and there are always more people getting soaked than there are people receiving benefits.

subtopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, realizing that Bill S-31 was to come before the house during this hour I looked for the evidence before the standing committee and, like my hon. friend from Timiskaming, I was unable to find it.

April 13, 1967
Private Bills
Apparently it is not in print yet. My hon. friend did have the opportunity of attending the hearing before the committee but I was not able to do so and I am therefore somewhat at a loss in considering the merits of the bill now before us in committee of the whole house.
However, as I examined the title of the bill I discovered it to be "An Act respecting the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company". This rang a bell in my mind and I recalled that I had been a member of the old committee of the house on railways, canals and telegraph lines some ten years ago when a similar measure was under consideration. So I looked at the statutes of 1956 and examined chapter 68 entitled "An Act respecting the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company". I found there were some interesting similarities between that bill and the bill now before us. Both bills contain only one clause, the clause now before us, and I believe the differences and similarities between them may be of interest to hon. members who were not present when chapter 68 was enacted in 1956.
Clause 1 of the bill now before us reads:
Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company, hereinafter called "the Company", may within a period of ten years from the 14th day of May, 1967, complete that portion of its line of railway authorized by chapter 80 of the statutes of 1947 which is not now completed, namely, from the town of Schefferville, in the province of Quebec, to Ungava Bay, and, if within the said period the said line of railway is not completed and put in operation, the powers of construction conferred upon the Company by the Parliament of Canada shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the said line of railway as then remains uncompleted.
This is what is set out in chapter 68 of the statutes of 1956:
Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company, hereinafter called "the Company", may within a period of ten years from the 14th day of May, 1957, complete that portion of its line of railway authorized by chapter 80 of the statutes of 1947 which is not now completed, namely, from the town of Schefferville, in the province of Quebec, to Ungava Bay, and, if within the said period the said line of railway is not completed and put in operation, the powers of construction conferred upon the Company by the Parliament of Canada shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the said line of railway as then remains uncompleted.
It will be obvious to hon. members that save for the fact that the date is changed from May 14, 1957 to May 14, 1967 the bill now before us is identical in its terms with that which was before us ten years ago. This leads me to wonder whether this is likely to

be a hardy decennial bill which will come before parliament every ten years from now until we celebrate our second centenary. In view of the fact that ten years after its earlier application the company is apparently in the same position with respect to the extension of this railway as it was in 1956, one wonders whether there is really much point in renewing this charter in respect of the portion of the line which still remains to be constructed.
If my understanding is correct as to what was said before the committee by a spokesman for the railway company, the company has indicated that it has no present intention of completing the line of railway to Ungava Bay within the next ten years. This is what I have been told. It seems to me that when the company comes before parliament with a request of this kind it should have serious intentions because undoubtedly the terms of this bill do confer rights and privileges and its passage may have an impact on other concerns and interests and what they may wish to do or be able to do within this large area of Canada. Having renewed the company's privileges for one period of ten years during which they apparently were not exercised, it seems to me the house should do nothing more now than extend the company's rights in respect of projects it has every intention of fulfilling.
When I realized that this bill was in terms almost identical with the one introduced ten years ago, I took the trouble to refresh my mind as to what had gone on in the committee when the earlier application was under consideration. In the proceedings of the house committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines in 1956 we find that Mr. Hugh E. O'Donnell, Q.C., solicitor for the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company, appeared as a witness. He had this to say, as reported at page 10 of the committee evidence:
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, this is a very simple bill.
I do not know why it is that all these bills that come in as private bills are always described as being very simple bills. Whether this is because they consider that members of the House of Commons are a bit simple minded and can only cope with simple bills, I have never been able to decide. Mr. O'Donnell continued:
It is merely asking for authority to extend the franchise for a further ten years. The railway was incorporated, as hon. members know, in 1947 and its purpose was to permit the construction of a railway from a point on the St. Lawrence River to Ungava Bay.
April 13, 1967



Then he went on to describe the route of the railway, which was shown on a map placed in a position where members of the committee could see it. He pointed out that-
[DOT]-it runs from Seven Islands to Schefferville which is 375 miles; 138 miles roughly from the river to the southern boundary of Labrador and then for a distance of 212 miles across Labrador and back into Quebec at Schefterville which is approximately 25 miles beyond; there is approximately 300 miles from Schefferville to Ungava Bay, and at the present time there is no requirement for transportation in that area.
Then a little later on we had before us Mr. W. H. Durrell, the vice president and general manager of the Iron Ore Company of Canada. The then hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, now Hon. Howard Green, was a member of the committee and he questioned Mr. Durrell as follows, at page 14 of the evidence:
By Mr. Green:
Q. Your company built this railway in order to get out your own iron ore deposits in the vicinity of Schefferville?-A. That is right.
Q. That is the real and only reason that you constructed the railway?-A. We had sufficient tonnage to justify the building of the railway.
Q. Have you any rights north of Schefferville towards Ungava Bay?-A. Yes. Our company and our subsidiaries are doing a lot of work in that region. When you say 'rights', you mean ground?
Q. Yes?-A. We have a subsidiary company called Orlando mines which spent several million dollars in the last few years to justify the extension of the railway.
Q. Would you please point out on the map where you have these deposits and rights north of Schefferville?-A. On this ground we staked the same as any other prospector.
He went on to point out that at Fort McKenzie they have a small copper showing. Mr. Green then asked:
Q. What other companies or groups have rights, or are working in that area between Schefferville and Ungava Bay?-A. They are about here on the map at this point, south of the Koksoak River, and Fentimore iron is in there. They will be doing considerable work with their base metal concessions. Mr. Chairman, I feel everything has been said which could be said about Bill No. S-31, entitled an Act respecting Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company. Still, I noticed what the hon. members for Timiskaming and Comox-Alberni (Messrs. Peters and Barnett) had to say.
I do not think that the company concerned, or the other companies, because there are others operating in that area-

I should like to say to my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni, in respect of his statement that for the past 10 years, or at the time when

Mr. Green gave evidence before the committee in 1956, everything was frozen, that there has been a great deal of movement in that part of the country in question. As you know, this was started by one company, the Iron Ore Company of Canada. Three very large companies are operating up in that area now.
From Schefferville to Ungava Bay there are 282 miles of country in which at the present time there is absolutely nothing. I do not believe this company should be forced to build a railway 282 miles in length for the caribou. With the development which is going on in that area, we have no assurance that some other company will not ask for a charter to build a railroad in that part of the Ungava and Labrador area. I do not see anything in this bill which suggests that with this 10 year extension this area will be frozen.
The proof of this is that we have seen the Wabush mines develop the Wabush area. They built their own railroad on a 42 mile stretch which connected with the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway which comes down to Seven Islands. This railroad was built, even though this clause in respect of the 10 years existed at that time.

subtopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question. He said that another railway company could come to parliament and obtain a charter. This I believe was in respect of the unbuilt line of railway from Schefferville to Ungava Bay. Is the hon. member seriously suggesting that another company could come along, ask for a charter, and then take the risk of building a railroad through that distance of undeveloped country which he mentioned? I am sure he knows the country much better than I do, although I did fly over it last summer while on the way to Frobisher. Is he seriously suggesting this would happen when another company has been given by parliament the right to build a competing line running parallel to it?
I have another question which has to do with the area he mentioned, where the Wabush Mining Company has its railway. Does he not feel, because of the charter granted by parliament to this particular company, that it would have a big hand in negotiations with another company in respect of an extension to that line? Does he not feel that this charter extension gives this particular company an unfair advantage, if it wished to use it, in its relations with another company which might wish to develop a mine?

subtopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY

Mr. Chairman, in answer to the first question, as this area between Schef-ferville and Ungava Bay is entirely in the province of Quebec, if because of economic developments some company wished to build a railroad there, they would not have to come to the Canadian parliament; they would just have to go to the Quebec parliament and obtain a private charter in the same way the Quebec-Cartier Mining Company did. They are private carriers; they are not common carriers because they are operating in one province only.
In respect of the second question, I do not think the charter of the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company has prevented the Wabush mines developing this large area, because so far that company has invested $295 million and another $112 million in their pelletizing plant at Sept-lies. I should like to repeat that even though this clause in respect of the 10 year period is in existence I do not think, if economic developments warranted the building of a railroad, that anybody else who wished to build a railroad would be prevented from doing so. They would merely have to apply to the Quebec parliament for a charter, and obtain it.

The original charter was granted in respect of a line to Ungava, because of the desire to have access to a seaport. At that time the engineers said that the only way to ship this ore through a deep sea port was by building a line to Fort Chimo on Ungava Bay. Since then the engineering studies have indicated that this ore can be shipped feasibly over a rail line from Schefferville to Seven Islands. That is what is being suggested at the present time.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)

subtopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill was considered extensively by a committee. The officials of the Iron Ore Company appeared and told in a straightforward way about their future plans for the development of that area. I was very much impressed with their testimony and the story they told about this development in Quebec and Labrador. As one who does not know very much about the area, let me say I think this is an interesting idea and I support their request for a 10 year extension.
Some information was given today by an hon. member to my left to the effect that this company was asking for an exclusive franchise or a blank cheque. Actually the company is asking for nothing more than a 10 year extension. They have indicated the difficulties involved in this whole project, and that apparently no other company seems to have an interest. That to me is significant. I recall asking the representatives of that company during a committee hearing whether there was any such interest. If we do not grant this extension and take away this franchise we will do a disservice to this area because the rail line may never be built. In view of that fact I for one want to indicate my interest and personal support in respect of this request for an extension.

subtopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question? If I understood him correctly, he made some reference to a statement made by an hon. member in this area of the house. Is the hon. member trying to suggest that the concern expressed by Hon. Howard Green ten years ago was concern expressed through the top of his hat? I am not suggesting that Howard Green was not interested in the development of that area, but he certainly expressed some concern originally about the kind of action proposed by this bill.

subtopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY

Mr. Chairman, I was probably a member of the committee at that time, though I do not remember the particular hearing to which the hon. member has referred. Presumably Mr. Green was his usual optimistic self at that time, but things did not work out as expected. Surely we should not criticize his optimism. The only thing I objected to in the hon. member's statement was his reference to a blank cheque. By adopting this bill we will not be issuing a blank cheque. All we will be doing is extending the company's right to continue

something in which nobody else seems to be interested.

subtopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is all right to suggest that this charter does not have an exclusive aspect, but every time a property is discovered with some valuable ore deposits, this company will be able to dictate who can develop that property, just as the Wabush Company has done. Anybody who appreciates the troubles between the Wabush Company and the Iron Ore Company of Canada must be aware that this whole matter is not a simple one. We gave that company the absolute right to say who is going to operate a mine in the area in which it is located.
If we do the same thing in respect of the company in question no prospector will go into that area looking for whatever resource properties may exist there, because he will not be able to develop them without building a rail line at a construction cost of perhaps $500,000 per mile. We will in effect be allowing this company to decide what arrangement may be made for the development of this area. It may well go to the provincial government for a charter as a common carrier, in order to develop its own holdings.
Surely it is apparent that this company no longer intends to do what it originally had in mind. In the original charter it was stated that if within set periods the line of rail was not commenced or completed and put into operation the power in respect of construction conferred upon the company by the parliament of Canada would cease, and be null and void in respect of that part of the said line which remained incomplete. The company agreed that if it did not build the line outlined in the charter it would not have control of the construction of the remainder.
I am in agreement with the hon. member that the company found it extremely expensive to build a line in order to have a deep sea port on Ungava Bay. For that reason the company decided not to use that area as a shipping point. Almost all line construction now leads to Seven Islands, and the company is not at all interested in developing this other portion.
Surely there is no reason for extending this charter for another ten years. The hon. member for Skeena suggested that this company should put up a performance bond in the amount of $10 million, or $1 million per year for ten years. That amount of money would finance the construction of an additional 20 miles of line. Surely that is not an un-

reasonable amount in light of the fact that some 220 miles of line is contemplated. That is not an extravagant requirement.
Originally we gave this company an opportunity to develop this rail line in a certain area. There is an inherent commitment on the part of the company. I predict that within a short period of time the company will come back to this house or to the provincial government asking for another extension in respect of another 60 miles of rail line to be built in another direction. The original charter was quite explicit as to where the line was to be built, although the company was given a great deal of leeway.
It is my opinion that if we grant this extension the company will build rail lines in directions other than the one originally contemplated. While I have no objection to giving this company the right to develop their property or to construct a rail line, I believe the people of Canada should not allow it to develop its rail lines in a disorderly fashion-a short piece of line going this way, another piece going that way, and still another going another direction.
For the various reasons I have outlined I think this company should be required to abide by the original injunction to which it agreed in 1947. If the company is prepared to make a commitment similar to what has been suggested, I am prepared to support this bill. The very fact that they have not suggested a performance bond is an indication that the company has little interest in the extension of this line as originally contemplated.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I was discussing several of the seven points which I believe are at issue in this very vital debate. If I may review them briefly, they concern the effect on morale of the proposed unification bill, the so-called savings about which the minister has been talking, and the so-called increase in efficiency which will result from unification. I mentioned briefly the issue of conscription, and what we mean by the expression "unification of the armed services".
Now I should like to go on to discuss briefly the sixth point, namely whether or not the unification proposed by the minister and the government will create any incompatability between our armed services and the armed services of other countries. Let me refer once again to the committee's proceedings which, at page 1320, contain a remark by General Moncel in response to a question by the hon. member for Queens. It reads as follows:

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext: Do you believe that our oportunity to gain from the experience and resources of our allies, which you mentioned some time ago in reply to a previous question-chiefly, Great Britain and the United States-will be lessened if we have an entirely different organization in the form of a unified force?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
Of course, it will.
He goes on to give an example. From General Moncel's reply one gathers there will be a great lessening in the amount of interplay that can go on properly between the armed services of this country and the armed services primarily of Great Britain and the United States. Yet the minister still persists in pointing out how efficient we are going to be if we have a force which will be, as he says, truly Canadian, with one uniform but no Royal Canadian Navy, no Royal Canadian Air Force and no Canadian Army: Just the Canadian forces. But is this realistic? Can we, so to speak, go it alone? Can we have an armed force, unique in every sense of the word, but different from the armed forces of our allies? Do we plan to fight our own wars or do we plan to let somebody else do the fighting for us? Is this the type of attitude 23033-942
National Defence Act Amendment that Canada exhibited during the last two wars? Of course it is not. But is it the minister's plan for the future? We are being inundated with plans for the future.
I read a rather interesting article in last night's Ottawa Journal under the byline of Peter Newman. I think it is a very interesting comment which should go on the record. Mr. Newman says this:
It must be emphasized that none of these startling ideas are in the process of becoming government policy. They reflect only the serious questioning that's going on about Canada's military future.
A little later I will explain why I feel it is worth putting this article on the record, but let me diverge for a moment. When I listened to the minister's speech the other night I could not help but be struck by the similarity between the article which appeared in Tuesday night's Ottawa Journal written by Mr. Peter Newman and the speech made by the minister. Far be it from me to suggest that there was any collusion between the minister and Mr. Peter Newman. I would never think of suggesting such a thing; but the fact is they were both discussing in exactly the same way-and the words are indeed very close-the relationship between Mr. McNamara and the joint chiefs of staff in the United States. With this background, and realizing that there appears to be some rapport of some kind, I would like to read the following excerpt from Mr. Newman's article:
A much more dramatic break with Canadian military tradition is being advocated by some of Ottawa's younger Liberals. They want, in effect, to demilitarize our unified armed forces-
Let hon. members note that the services are already unified in their view.
-and turn them into an economic instrument. This would mean moving young men into temporary service in the armed forces during periods of economic recession,-
I have no doubt that the government is afraid of exactly that in the near future. It goes on to read:
-giving them trade training while they serve, and letting them rejoin the labour force when jobs become available again.
This is what the government is planning for the armed forces of our country. It continues:
At the same time, the Department of National Defence would be turned into the headquarters-
And this is the piece de resistance.
-for a sort of domestic and foreign peace corps.
This is an incredible summation for a journalist who over the past few years seems to
April 13, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment have had a tremendous affinity for hon. gentlemen opposite. I am sure that Mr. Newman would not think of writing anything in the Ottawa Journal, or any of the other papers which carry his column, which did not have a large element of truth in it. Imagine, Mr. Chairman, turning our armed forces into an economic instrument.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
What about our commitments? The most important point of all is our ability to meet our commitments with a unified force. Many references were made in the evidence to this point. As reported at page 1384, Air Marshal Annis pointed out that he did not believe that with a unified force we could carry on our present commitments under NATO, NORAD and so on. As reported at page 1312 General Moncel said exactly the same thing, Let me just quote briefly what he said in reply to the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, whose name I understand is familiar to the minister:
-I will write you a commitment tor the country which will generate the need for a unified force. It is very simple. But with your current commitments you do not want one. In fact, it Is better that you do not have one.
Air Vice Marshal Hendrick gave evidence on this point at page 1451 of the report. Lieutenant General Moncel dealt with it again, as reported at page 1323. He was asked this question by the hon. member for Greenwood:
Therefore, the real choice that we have to make, as a nation and that we are responsible for making in parliament, in the matter of making sense out of unification, is whether we are going to continue the roles that we have or concentrate on this mobile intervention force?
To that question General Moncel answered: "Yes".
I could draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to many more comments of this nature. I think it is interesting to note that General Moncel made a rather appropriate comment when he said that we were moving on an unchartered course at a very high speed toward an unknown destination. And guess who is at the helm, Mr. Chairman-a man with no navigation experience at all, the Minister of National Defence.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me, in view of the preponderance of evidence-

In view of the preponderance of evidence, which indicates that we should stand back and take a second look at what is going on here, I submit we should heed the advice of these experts who appeared before our defence committee and the minister should take time for sober second thoughts about this legislation.
