I think this is essential if we are to continue to be able to defend our country in the future as we have in the past.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to take part in this debate, but on listening to the minister's speech last Tuesday afternoon it seemed to me there was an indication that he might be mellowing just a bit. Since I have had the pleasure of knowing the minister personally for a number of years, I thought that if I stood up and made a personal plea to him to reconsider his position he might do just that. I have known the minister, as I said, for a number of years and had always thought that he was an understanding and tolerant man. Regrettably I must say that some of his recent actions and some of his not so recent actions could well indicate otherwise.
I want to talk for a little while about integration and then about that now infamous word, unification. I am not going to speak on the subject with the degree of authority that someone who has considerable military experience might. I do not pretend to be an expert. However, I do have some views to express, mainly because I have had the opportunity of discussing this issue with many people right across Canada. I have talked to people of all ages, people with military experience and otherwise, people in the army, the navy, the air force and civilians.
I agree, I say at once, with the principle of integration. I think there are services that
April 13, 1367

operate economically and efficiently under integration-for example, hospital services, medical services, chaplain services, administration, and in some respects supply services. They can be and are integrated, with a saving of some considerable consequence. I am sure that with research and with a little greater knowledge of the subject I could make many suggestions where like savings could be effected. I also believe that practical business procedures should not be foreign to defence administration and that the application of some business sense and business law can effect some significant savings in the long run.
Getting back to this infamous word unification, Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that the minister does not know what the word means. The previous chairman of the defence committee was not sure what it meant when he spoke in this house Tuesday last, April 11.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if you take away from servicemen the identification of their skills, the uniform that identifies them with a specific service, and you give all servicemen a pea-green uniform, then you have nothing left. You have no meaning or symbol; you have no tradition; you have no history. You really have no meaningful defence posture. I suggest that in his haste the minister is willing to sacrifice all of this identity because he wants at all costs to create this new warrior as his personal centennial project; and for the sake of the minister I hope that he is right and that he knows what he is doing.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
The minister is not altogether without friends. I read the white paper when it came out in March of 1964. In April of that year I was invited to speak to a service club in Edmonton, and at that time I tried to show some of the anomalies and inadequacies in the proposal. The only newspaper in Edmonton, The Edmonton Journal, on April 9, 1964, took it upon itself to criticize me for expressing a view on the matter. I have the editorial before me. Subsequent action and the introduction of legislation proved that my initial contention was correct. The editorial said:
Mr. William Skoreyko made some reasonable criticisms of the new defence proposals, when he spoke to the Macdonald-Cartier Club here, but he also fell into a number of careless or Inaccurate statements-
What Mr. Hellyer has emphasized over and over again, and what is a central theme of his white paper, is that housekeeping costs are to be reduced so that a higher percentage of the defence budget can be devoted to the purchase of capital equipment.

National Defence Act Amendment
I agree with the sentiment of the last sentence. It continues:
At another point in his talk, Mr. Skoreyko tried to make a problem out of the proposed gradual conversion of the fourth brigade (in reverse in Canada) "into a special service force."
We quote the white paper's wording. He asked how the three services would feel, after being jumbled into one force, when they see a new force created with special uniforms and name.
Mr. Skoreyko sees something that isn't there. We take the white paper and the minister to mean, simply, a force or unit for special service. Who, apart from Mr. Skoreyko, has suggested that it would have a special uniform?
I do not wish to criticize the editorial writers of the newspaper, though I know something of their political backgrounds. I would not ask the minister to communicate with them, telling them to write another editorial to tell the people of Edmonton that the previous editorial was wrong, that the minister has now decided on a pea-green uniform. The editorial goes on to say:
By no means all Mr. Skoreyko's statements are open to criticism. But in so vital a matter as a radical change in defence policy he ought to be certain that none of his remarks is careless, inaccurate or misleading. Defence is much too important to be left to confusion.
I agree with the last paragraph. But that newspaper is not justified in asking us to refrain from speaking when the responsibility for unification or integration is that of the present Minister of National Defence.
Turning to another subject, I listened with considerable interest to the minister's speech of last Tuesday afternoon. Most of us, when we are apt to be affected politically have short memories, but I wish to refer to a paragraph on page 14788 of Hansard of last Tuesday afternoon, in which the Minister of National Defence attacked the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. The minister said:
The second example I should like to give is the choice of the airplane for the strike role; I am referring to the CF-104. Here again, Mr. Chairman, there is a very unusual sequence of events. The choice that was made of the CF-104 was a government decision. It is true that eventually the chiefs of staff made a recommendation, but only after they had been directed to do so by the government-
Who, does the minister think, should have directed the chiefs of staff, if they needed directing?
-of the right hon. gentleman and only after they had already said that this was not the best airplane to carry out the role and was in fact not suitable to carry out the role.
It is interesting, when reading the clippings, to see that the minister does not enjoy
April 13, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment the cleanest record when it comes to taking advice from people in authority in the defence structure.
I have in my hand a clipping headed, "Hellyer Rejected Plane Advice". To me that means that the Minister of National Defence is putting himself above a prime minister of a country. The minister says that the prime minister, obviously in 1961 or 1962, rejected the advice of the chiefs of staff and bought an aircraft. The present Minister of National Defence rejected advice, and he also bought an aircraft. The article says this:
Hon. Paul Hellyer, minister of defence, rejected the recommendation of most of his senior military advisers when he decided on purchase of a fighter-bomber.
Informed sources made the disclosure Tuesday.
However, the sources added, the senior officers did not resent rejection of their advice nor did Mr. Hellyer question their ability in making it. Such decisions were up to the government and the military accepted them.
The minister sits on the government benches today; it is all right for him to recommend certain things to the chiefs of staff, but it is not all right for the former Conservative prime minister to have advised his chiefs of staff. This is an interesting article. It continues:
Air Chief Marshal Frank Miller, chief of the defence staff, issued a statement Tuesday denying a Canadian Press report Monday that Air ViceMarshal Wilfred Bean was transferred to Europe because he opposed purchase of the CF-5.
Perhaps the minister will take the opportunity to answer that charge:
The statement did not deny that Air Vice Marshal Bean had opposed acquisition of the CF-5. It described his posting overseas to 4th Allied Tactical Air Force as routine. He had been assistant chief of defence staff.
Informants said Air Chief Marshal Miller and Air Marshal Clare Annis, chief of logistics, as well as Air Vice Marshal Bean, favored purchase of the American McDonnell Phantom jet fighter-bomber on strictly military grounds.
They noted that Air Chief Marshal Miller did not attend the press conference at which Mr. Hellyer announced choice of the CF-5 though he had attended a similar press briefing in December when selection of other defence equipment was announced by the minister.
One can see the degree of co-operation existing as early as August 25, 1965.
Another interesting point in this article is that the CF-5 program of up to 125 aircraft made by Canadair Limited, Montreal, is relatively cheap, as such weapons programs go:
While the decision to turn down the Phantom and buy the CF-5 was in the long process of being made, the objections of senior officers to the latter plane filtered down through the RCAF, officials said.

As a result, they said, a major "selling job" had to be done among men who would fly and maintain the plane. There are already two Nor-throp-made CF-5s at Cold Lake, Alta., the RCAF's big jet training base, for demonstration purposes.
Northrop has made no secret of the fact it accepted an extremely low payment-
It does not matter how cheap an aircraft is. Another article that I have describes the CF-E as a peashooter.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I wish to refer to another editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune of April 12, 1967. It read in part:
More than one year ago John Diefenbaker asked for an investigation of the proposed purchase of CF-5 aircraft to cost $215 million. The leader of the opposition made the demand because of continual changes in the assessed capacity of this plane.
Briefly it had already been established that the CF-5 had:
(a)	No capability as a fighter.
(b)	No interceptor use.
(c)	No long-range capacity.
(d)	Could not be refueled in the air without expensive tanker aircraft.
(e)	No ability to take off from improvised fields with a bomb load.
(f)	No adaptability for close support as a bom-ber-strafer.
(g)	And deemed useless by the U.S. air force for service in Viet Nam without costly modifications.
Yet the minister criticized the present Leader of the Opposition for adopting the CF-104 which had been developed by the Liberals and which, as I am sure he will now admit, has done excellent service in NATO and elsewhere.
This is not all that has been said about the CF-5. An article which appeared in the Edmonton Journal, written by Charles Lynch and headed "Combat Tests on Tap for RCAF's New Jet" stated:
One of the embarrassing things about Canada's purchase of the American Freedom Fighter aircraft is that, to date, the United States hasn't bought any for its own use.
That is wrong, now. They have bought about 100. The article goes on:
Officials of our defence department have been saying all along that the U.S. intends to make such purchases, and that the United States Air Force desperately wants the Freedom Fighter, the Canadian name for which is the CF-5.
Now, the evidence is beginning to come in and the defence department is delighted.
What's happened is that the U.S.A.F. has persuaded Defence Secretary Robert McNamara, long a sceptic about the Freedom Fighter, to send 20 of the planes to Viet Nam for combat testing. Later,
April 13, 1967

in the fall, they will go to Viet Nam for strafing and bombing missions.
The writer goes on to say:
After all, the Tories turned down an earlier version of the Freedom Fighter in 1959, and it is unlikely that they will applaud the government's purchase of it now.
That is very true. How could we?
Freedom Fighters for Viet Nam cost $700,000 apiece, somewhat lower than the starting price in Canada of $900,000 each which would be inflated by other charges.
In the words of one Washington dispatch, the Freedom Fighter might well serve as a better peashooter than some of the planes now in Viet Nam. I should like to hear a little more about this fantastic aircraft, in the light of the hon. gentleman's criticism of the CF-104.
With reference again to the minister's speech of Tuesday, April 11: After an exchange of words with the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. gentleman said-and he was referring to my right hon. friend:
He was not going to be pushed around by the Industrial military complex. He was going to show who was running Canada and cancel the Avro Arrow regardless.
Well, it seems the Minister of National Defence is not going to be pushed around by anyone. I will come back to that later.
If hon. members would refer to Saturday Night of March 1965 they will find there an article written by Kenneth McNaught which states, in part:
My conclusion is that the Liberals never really wanted to accept nuclear weapons, that they did so in order not to upset their principal supporters in the business community, who were worried about the possible effects of our recalcitrance on economic relations with the United States, and that we are now seeking a way out of the nuclear commitment.
Here he is saying that the Leader of the Opposition did not wish to be pushed around and thought it best that he cancel the Avro Arrow because it did not fit well into the economy. Because he did this he was showing that he did not intend to be pushed around. But the Minister of National Defence did not intend to be pushed around, either, because in 1962 he spoke up in the House of Commons, as only he could, in favour of a policy of no nuclear weapons for Canada. Then he changed his mind.
I wish to speak for a few moments about the veracity of this government and of the minister. We are now asked to believe the government when it says that all is well in
National Defence Act Amendment the armed forces. We should have no doubt about the government's sincerity in connection with Bill C-243. But we have had considerable experience with this government. The desire to get elected was a major reason for some startling changes in their attitude a few years ago. But sincerity is not something which one practices only when it is convenient.
I have here an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune of February 13, 1963 and I think it should once again be placed on record because it is a most interesting article. It begins:
The Liberals are the most bewildered and bewildering of all the four parties on the nuclear issue. Statements by Lester Pearson and Paul Hellyer after the Liberal council meeting this week have added to the confusion.
This is not surprising. It is in keeping with the party's attitude for the past four years.
Since 1960 the Liberals have been against nuclear weapons and for nuclear weapons; they have been partly against nuclear weapons and partly for nuclear weapons; they have been against nuclear weapons in Canada but maybe for nuclear weapons for Canadian NATO forces in Europe.
Here are some highlights in the Liberal record:
Paul Hellyer, Liberal defence critic, announced his party's defence program in the Commons on August 4, 1960. The main points were no nuclear weapons for use on Canadian soil or in Canadian air space; scrap plans to acquire the Starfighter for Canada's NATO forces; scrap the Bomarc-SAGE program for anti-bomber defence of this continent.
[DOT] (8:40 pun.)
That was a noble stand.
The following day Mr. Pearson said in the Commons:
"In my view we should get out of the whole SAGE-Bomarc operation, and we should not spend any more money on radar gap fillers. Our objection to the Bomarc is not only that we do not think it is an effective weapon ... our objection is the kind of defence strategy it represents and which we do not think will be effective, however effective the weapon may be. If the United States wishes to continue that kind of protection, let the United States do so. Let us withdraw from that direct form of continental defence."
That is also a noble statement.
The Liberal leader took a different attitude toward "commitments" at that time.
Mr. Pearson went on to say, "After all, this kind of defence is primarily a United States responsibility. It is the defence of the deterrent. We know how important that is; but it is a deterrent which is under the sole control of the United States of America."
Nor was the Liberal leader much concerned about anti-Americanism, for he continued, "It is not a defence, and in the nature of things I submit it cannot be a defence, of our territory in the traditional sense of the word, and it will soon be no defence of anything ... It seems to me, Mr. April 13, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment Chairman, that our experience in the past three years has shown that in attempting to participate in continental defence in the way we have, we are becoming nothing more than just the last two knots on the Bomarc tail of the defence kite."
I do not need to tell the committee what happened only weeks after he made those statements. For the benefit of hon. members on the other side who were not here at the time and would like to read the record, they will find it at page 7606 of Hansard for August 5, 1960. This seemed to be the Liberal party position until January 12, 1963, when the Prime Minister visited Toronto and had this to say at a meeting of the York-Scar-borough Liberal Association:
"It (the Ottawa government) should end its evasion of responsibility, by discharging the commitments it has already accepted for Canada. It can only do this by accepting nuclear warheads, for those defensive tactical weapons which cannot effectively be used without them, but which we have agreed to use. An agreement with the United States for this purpose would have to be negotiated-
That was on January 12. A few days later it was not negotiation he spoke about. He said it should be reviewed. I do not need to put any more of this article on the record, Mr. Chairman.
I again point out one simple fact. The Minister of National Defence is asking us to accept his word that everything is all right so far as Canada's defence structure is concerned. His attitude is, "We will look after the armed forces. Leave it to us. Pass the bill and let us get ahead with the job." All I say is that we have had considerable experience with the government. We have had considerable experience with the Prime Minister. We have had considerable experience with the veracity of the Minister of National Defence. I am not sure that as a member of parliament I want to turn over to him the sole responsibility of taking care of an essential part of our country's defence.
How confident is the minister that the program he has embarked on is the right one? I suppose any normal human being, after making a statement of fact in the House of Commons, would assume that, if it was a statement on a subject of vital interest to Canadians, they would read it in the press, and if further interested they would find ways and means of obtaining more information relative to the subject. That is nbt the case with the Minister of National Defence. He made a speech in the House of Commons, and then to make sure it was read, though it really did not matter whether it was read or
[Mr. Skoreyko.l
not, he went out and spent $5,398 of the taxpayers' money to make sure that it was read. I quote this report from the Edmonton Journal of March 14:

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, you know I am the soul of brevity and I just wish to take two or three minutes to correct some inaccurate information given to the press last evening by Mr. Lee who, I understand, is the information officer for the minister's office. Yesterday I asked the minister this question, as recorded at page 14829 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. I am informed that a dozen chief petty officers and petty officers from the Royal Canadian Navy, coming from the east and west coasts, are attending a supply course in the district. As one feature of that course they are present in the gallery of this chamber. Before coming here they were told to remove their uniforms because the unification debate will be taking place and it would not be appropriate for them to be in naval uniform on this occasion. Can the minister explain this situation?
April 13, 1967	COMMONS
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, not only am I unable to explain it, I had not heard about it until this moment.
I will make inquiries.
However, as soon as I had asked the question Mr. Lee went around to the press and to the radio people in the house and informed them that the reason these men were not allowed in the house in their uniforms was because this was a tradition from the time of Charles I. While there was no law in this respect-he had consulted the legal office of the minister's department-it was a tradition and a practice in all parliaments of the Commonwealth.
This is quite incorrect. During my experience here of nearly 22 years I have never seen a member of the armed forces denied admission to the galleries. I have made inquiries since yesterday and I can truly say that no Speaker and no Sergeant-at-Arms has ever issued an order that members of the armed forces who come to the galleries, unarmed and in uniform, shall be denied entrance to the galleries of the house. The same rule applies to the mother of parliaments.
As a matter of fact I was at Westminster in Great Britain when, for one moment, being a member of parliament from Canada I was what is known as a distinguished visitor. The procedure is that you line up and your name is called. In front of me was an admiral of the Royal Navy in full uniform and we sat together in the distinguished visitors gallery of the house, one of my brief moments of glory in a rather mediocre career.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Anyway the practice is the same in the mother of parliaments. Last evening I was asked to appear on television at a private television station. I made some comments on this matter. One of the members of the press finally came to me with the statement made by Mr. Lee. 1 said this was nonsense. Strangely enough a gentleman who stays at the University Club of Toronto immediately wrote me as follows:
Dear Mr. Herridge: I have just heard on "The World at Six" C.B.C. radio program of your hassle with Mr. Hellyer over his ruling that it was improper under a tradition going back to Charles I for military or naval personnel to appear in the gallery of the House of Commons in uniform.
Of course it was not a hassle with the minister; it was a question of something
National Defence Act Amendment which originated with the minister's information officer, parliamentary assistant and chief factotum. The letter continues:
This is nonsense. In 1917, after being wounded and invalided home, I was for a year private secretary to Sir Edward Kemp then minister of militia and defence in the Borden government. In September or October of that year I sat on the floor of the house in uniform, in front of the minister, during the debate on the Military Service Act providing for conscription. The gallery was liberally sprinkled with officers and other ranks of the army and navy-no Canadian air force then existed-all in uniform.
The reason for my presence was that I had assisted in drafting the bill which was finalized by the late Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, then solicitor general, who steered it through the house.
The late Major Gen. Eugene Fiset, then deputy minister, later Lieutenant Governor of Quebec, would normally have been on the floor on that occasion and had, of course, been there many times during the war years always in full uniform.
It looks as if Mr. Hellyer has pulled another boner.
Yours sincerely, Everett Bristol, late Major 15 Bn. 1st Can. Div.
He is quite mistaken. It was not a boner on the part of the minister; it was a boner on the part of the gentleman behind the scenes. However, I am sure all of us, the minister and everyone in this house regardless of party, welcomes members of the armed forces of Canada to the galleries of this chamber. I am very pleased to see that Mr. Lee's decision already has been revised, because in the gallery behind me are two members of the Royal Canadian Navy in uniform.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, many members have been prompted to speak for various reasons. My reason for speaking is the fact that I completely agree with the Minister of National Defence on the principle-

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
Wait until you hear the rest of it-on the principle that it is the civilian authority which runs the nation and not the military. This is a principle which I believe the minister has enunciated more than once. I completely agree with him. I do not see how any Canadian could disagree with him on that score. History has shown us that in any nation, where the army or the military forces
April 13, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment have taken over the government, civil freedom and civil liberties naturally were kicked out the window. I also wish to speak in respect of Bill C-243 as a Canadian expressing a civilian point of view. I have listened with interest to what gentlemen on both sides of the house have had to say. I attended some meetings of the committee on national defence and have read very faithfully the comments which have appeared in the press.
As a Canadian with near relatives who have served this country as members of the forces I am as confused as some of the gentlemen who have spoken during the last number of days. I am confused, and I believe people in the rest of Canada are confused by the very fact that there is such a divergence of opinion between the Minister of National Defence and those who either were fired from the forces, or left before their normal retirement period. I am referring to those men who performed a distinguished service to this country as members of the army, navy or air force. These men who have served this nation well do not agree with the proposal submitted by the Minister of National Defence and his government. What axe do these men have to grind? Is this what one might call a conspiracy against the government? I do not think so; I do not think they are doing this for political reasons. They simply do not believe in this policy.
Whose judgment should the people of Canada accept? Should they accept the judgment of these distinguished men who have been in the services or the judgment of the government which is proposing something altogether new? This is confusing. Another thing which leads me to believe there must be some substance in this is that on the opposition side we have men who have distinguished themselves in the army or the navy, and have served this country well. These men are of the opinion that this policy of unifying our forces and making them into one force is not to the advantage of this nation and is not something which will provide a proper defence for this nation. Whom should the people of Canada believe?
I even have had a letter from a constituent who wonders why green was chosen as the colour for the uniform. Why not yellow, white, grey, black or any other colour? If we were in Ireland and the Irish Republican army were dressed in green we would not be surprised; it is the Emerald Isle. I do not think that green is an attractive colour. I do not look at our stewardesses on the airplanes more than once now, because they are dressed

in green. They looked much better when they wore air force blue. Why, of all colours, did the minister choose green.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext: Would my friend like an answer to that question?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED

I did not choose it. The armed
forces have been responsible for the colour of the uniform, as they have in respect of all the other details related to the principles we have been discussing in this house. Surely the hon. member would not wish to reflect on their choice. It was a spontaneous choice and they have been responsible for the development right from the outset.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
I will be putting more questions to the minister before I am through. One of my colleagues on this side of the house was considerably perturbed, and really wondered who was behind this and who conceived the idea of the unified force.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Who fathered the thought behind this program? My colleague did not want to give that honour to the Minister of National Defence, and I agree with him. I believe this idea was fathered by another gentleman who sits in the front benches. That gentleman holds the portfolio in the ministry of external affairs. He is a man who, during the last several years, has gone to great pains to establish peace in the world, and I take my hat off to him. He is an idealist and feels that Canada can play a great part in stamping out small conflagrations. He believes that Canada has a great part to play in policing the world. And we have considerable experience in this regard as a result of our efforts in the Gaza strip in keeping the Arabs and the Jews away from each other's throats.
Our boys have been stationed in various areas of the world, keeping the peace, and as things now are it looks as though they will be there forever. Hon. members of this house will recall that the Minister of National Defence jumped at the idea of sending our troops to keep the peace in Cyprus. The United Nations had no funds at that time and we had to shell out the money. This exercise
April 13, 1967	COMMONS
was supposedly to last tor three months, but our troops have been there for several years. The minister has been very quiet about this fact and has made no forecast as to how long they may be required; but the taxpayers are paying the shot. There is no hope of a settlement because presumably no steps are being taken to encourage a settlement, or at least the newspapers have not been reporting these steps.
The minister of external affairs has indicated that he hopes his peace efforts will be successful in Viet Nam, he is in favour of sending our boys to Viet Nam to keep the north and south Vietnamese from fighting. He believes in keeping peace in the world. I do not doubt the minister's sincerity, but I wonder why he feels that Canada should no longer worry about her own defence. That worry has been prompted by the words of the Minister of National Defence regarding the proposed mobile force which can be sent to any part of the world under the auspices of NATO, the United States or some other power.
The Minister of National Defence is becoming complacent about Canada's position, because of the considerable diminution of the cold war. We have all observed the outstretched hand from Moscow and we are not going to refuse to grasp those hands which offer friendship and peace. We have all listened to those friendly overtures from that red empire, which now occupies most of Europe. We have all heard of communist attempts to establish consulates in western countries, including Canada.
It is my belief that we are being hoodwinked by the cultural exchanges of communist students and students of the western world. We are beginning to believe that there is no longer any danger of difficulties with the U.S.S.R. It is my feeling that this is the belief of the minister of defence and the minister for external affairs. Apparently on that premise they have adopted this unification program.
Our position is becoming somewhat confused. We have spent a great deal of money in conjunction with the United States to set up a defence against the onslaught of the red army. We have spent a great deal of money in respect of our NATO efforts. I hasten to add that were it not for NATO many countries in Europe would not be free today. We will not refuse to grasp the hand of friendship. Before we place trust in the friendship of men like Kosygin and Brezhnev we should ask
National Defence Act Amendment them to go further to show their good intentions.
In this regard, Mr. Chairman, the Soviet union should remove the iron curtain and that abolish their border restrictions so that Canadians and citizens of other western countries can visit their lands, and in order that the people of those iron curtain countries can visit and even emigrate to western countries. These communist countries should allow the wives and children of people living in Canada to rejoin their families. Once they have shown that type of goodwill, perhaps we can accept their proffered friendship without restraint.
The right hon. leader of the official opposition suggested when he was prime minister that Khrushchev should free the 14 nations that compose the U.S.S.R. empire today. These people have different cultures, languages, and history. They should be allowed to vote freely, to retain their status in the union or to become independent. In this way the Russians could show their goodwill.
Apparently the Minister of National Defence is not concerned in this regard, but concerned only in grasping the outstretched hand. I suggest there is a good reason for this extension of friendship to the Americas by the U.S.S.R. That reason relates to the fact that officials in Moscow and Peking have ideological differences and are at loggerheads. Let us not forget that the Chinese have a claim against Russia in respect of some lost land in Siberia. The Chinese feel that Stalin was a good man and that the present-day officials in Moscow have torn him from his exalted position. One faction idealizes Khrushchev while the other does not. Let us never forget that neither of these two giants has renounced the idea of burying the western powers, just as Khrushchev suggested to the United States.
What will happen if these two great communist powers embrace each other again as they once did? They will likely march together hand in hand to capture the entire world. If that should take place the U.S.S.R. will again show its teeth by building a bigger wall in Berlin. If the worst happens Canada will become a buffer zone between the United States and the Soviet union. This will be the battleground between these two nations, and let us not fool ourselves in this regard. Which side will we join? I mean every word when I say that I would rather be clawed by the American eagle than crushed by the Russian bear.
April 13, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment [DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
One thing leads to another. We are pleased to see the world heading for what we think is peace. But is our force going to have no other duties to perform than policing difficult areas in the world? Are we going to have a force which will contribute to the defence of this nation? Have we no national pride? I believe that those gentlemen who have served in the forces, and the gentlemen on this side of the house who are opposing this bill so strenuously, deserve support; and I think they are getting a great deal of support in the country.
I received a telephone call just today. I asked the gentleman, a constituent of mine, "What is the reaction to this continuous debate on the unification bill?" He said, "Our request is, kill it." This is actual fact. I do not think we will kill it because the minister has sufficient guarantees from some of the smaller groups in the house to push the bill through; but he will not push it through until the country realizes what the bill means. Once the country realizes what it means, and that there is something rotten in the state of Denmark, the minister and the Liberal party will pay for it in the next election.
Ladies-excuse me, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext: There is one here.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
Yes, there is a lady here. Another point is economy. We heard a great deal from the minister a couple of years ago to the effect that it would be economical if we unified our forces. We do not hear so much about that today, because the estimates show that the minister's department is spending more than it ever did. Of course, that is the usual thing. That is what this government has been doing in every department. They talked about economy in 1963 and 1965, but that is now forgotten. Political promises are made only to be broken. That is the way this government has been carrying on. Where is the economy in this proposal? Canadians swallowed the idea that it might be more economical to have one unified force rather than providing supplies for three forces.
In 1966 the minister said that a survey was being made of our defence establishments with a view to cutting them down, and as soon as the survey was made a decision as to their future would be reached. There is no harm in having a survey. But when asked from time to time whether he had made his decision, the answer was always no, a decision had not been made. In spite of that, certain defence establishments were nibbled

away. I have in mind the one in my riding, the Canadian joint air training camp at Rivers. Personnel of the various units were moved out; they vacated the houses they had been renting in the area. Their children have had to get out of school. The population of that training establishment has been reduced, in spite of the fact that the minister says he has not made up his mind. When I placed a question on the order paper asking the minister when this establishment was going to be phased out, his answer was that it would not be done this year. But apparently it will be done some time in the future, if what his department is doing is any indication.
The minister should be honest and frank, just as frank as he was about the colour of the uniform, and tell these people what is to happen with that camp. Why prolong the agony? Why not tell them whether the establishment at Rivers is to be retained or phased out? The minister flew down there last fall in order to appease some of the vociferous Grits who were complaining, together with the Tories, that they wanted the issue brought to a head and wanted to find out whether this establishment was to be phased out. The minister neutralized some of the vociferous complaints, because these people are now keeping quiet. They trust that the minister will keep the establishment in operation, but it is being nibbled and nibbled away.
What function does this training establishment perform? It was set up in 1939. It has all the buildings and runways necessary for parachute-jump training. The river there has been dammed. There is a wonderful lake where the troops can practise jumps on the water. They have a joint school. The high school is only three miles from the base and it is at the disposal of the students at the base. Considerable sums of money from Ottawa were poured into the erection of the school at Rivers. The facilities at the base were not suitable or sufficient for the junior and elementary grades; they did not have the proper teaching staff, and these students have been attending the Rivers school.
What is the situation there today? I say that this establishment is being chiselled away. Rivers high school has lost 44 students because their parents have been moved to God knows where. The elementary school has suffered because two rooms are now receiving no school grant. We have in this small community 1,600 people. This establishment depended on defence dollars for its existence. I tell the minister quite frankly that today
April 13, 1957

there are 55-this is the situation today because I have today's statistics-houses and suites which stand empty. The people of Rivers built these houses for business purposes. They were rented by the personnel at the base. As I say, 55 houses and suites are now empty. Three houses built with the assistance of C.M.H.C. mortgages have been empty since last year. A house that cost $15,500 last year can be bought for $9,000 this year. I suggest that if the minister wants to retire somewhere in Canada he can buy a cheap house there. These people are going through the agony of uncertainty.
The minister tells us that the base will operate this year, but what will happen in 1968? This base has been nibbled and nibbled away and there will be nothing left in 1968. All the millions of dollars that were poured into the base to provide all these facilities will go to waste, Mr. Minister. Why is this? Why not be frank and tell the people what you are going to do?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext: He doesn't know.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
I agree that he doesn't
know. The survey has been carried out, but the minister has not yet made up his mind. I think he has made up his mind but will not tell us his decision. Last fall he made up his mind to receive a delegation from Rivers. The Minister of Defence Production was to set a date for the delegation to attend here. That date still has not been set, and these people are angry and unhappy.
That is all I have to say, Mr. Chairman, as a contribution to this debate. IMMIGRATION-REPORTED PRESENCE IN CANADA OF GERMAN WAR CRIMINALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 1 of this year there was a program on the C.B.C. with respect to certain nazi war criminals now living in Canada, which caused considerable concern to many persons who heard the program. Later on the same date a Canadian Press dispatch dealt at somewhat greater length with the question. I am going to quote the press dispatch so that the house may understand what I am talking about. It emanated from Ottawa and read:
Ottawa admits it got list of war criminals.
The External Affairs Department confirmed yesterday that a list of names of people alleged to be nazi war criminals living in Canada was given to the Canadian embassy in Vienna last year.
Simon Wiesenthal, the man who found Adolph Eichmann in Argentina in 1960, said in Toronto Friday that the names of 15 eastern Europeans who had committed crimes in Poland and the Baltic countries had been given to the embassy in Vienna about six months ago.
He said the people were not of serious consequence in the nazi hierarchy.
An External Affairs Department spokesman said Wiesenthal had handed the list of names to the embassy with no documentation. The names were sent to Ottawa where they were distributed to "the appropriate government departments."
He declined to say how many names were on the list.
The C.B.C. news report and this press dispatch have given concern to a good number of people and I have had letters on this subject and some phone calls from those persons who were concerned. To illustrate the concern of some Canadians with this situation I wish to quote one letter which I received: Dear Mr. Herridge,
I was quite shocked tonight to hear via the C.B.C. that we are harbouring at least 15 nazi war criminals in this country. The author of this statement is a chap called Wiesenthal, or reasonably close to this spelling, who operates out of an office in Vienna. He is Jewish and has dedicated his life to tracking down nazis who were and are responsible for many atrocities and he has had some considerable success. He claims that he advised the Canadian government of this fact some time ago but does not know if they have taken any action in this regard.
April 13, 1967	COMMONS
I would certainly like to have this matter raised in the house and can think of no one better equipped than yourself.

He was very concerned at that time that we were somewhat lax in allowing these people into the country. This is what the editorial had to say:
There is sound sense in what M. J. Coldwell, C.C.F. national leader, says in warning against letting fascist and nazi sympathizers immigrate to Canada. If as he claims too many of these people are getting in the department of immigration is at fault and should institute more rigorous checks.
We wouldn't accuse anyone in the department of being secretly sympathetic to totalitarian thinkers of this shade. Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, and I do so at the request of a number of persons who are quite concerned about this matter. In view of the statement made on the C.B.C. on April 1 by Mr. Simon Wiesenthal that Canada is harbouring at least 15 nazi war criminals and that he advised the Canadian government of this fact some time ago, has the minister been advised by Mr. Simon Wiesenthal of these war criminals being in Canada and, if so, what action does the minister Intend to take on this information?
I shall look forward to the reply to my question by the minister or by the person representing him here this evening. I shall be anxious to know what action the government is taking in an effort to locate these former nazi war criminals, because I believe, as I think a good many other members of this house and the Canadian people believe, that the sooner the government takes action to rid Canada of people of this type the better it will be for the maintenance of democracy today and in the years to come.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: IMMIGRATION-REPORTED PRESENCE IN CANADA OF GERMAN WAR CRIMINALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am informed that Mr. Wiesenthal did indeed come to Canada several weeks ago. He came to Toronto in connection with the release of his most recent book. Last summer Mr. Wiesenthal did, as the hon. member said, write to the Canadian embassy in Vienna to provide the embassy with the names, and in some cases the addresses, of people who he alleged were war criminals resident in Canada. The evidence respecting four out of approximately 12 such persons was considered by Mr. Wiesenthal to be particularly strong. He did not, however, supply our ambassador with detailed documentation concerning his allegations.
The information received from Mr. Wiesenthal was passed to other Canadian government departments, and the government departments concerned are continuing their examination of the general questions raised by the allegations that there are war criminals residing here. I am sure that the hon. member would be the first to agree that we should be governed by the system of law that we have in force, and, therefore it might be useful for him to know the exact circumstances under which these cases are considered.
A most careful study has been given to this matter and it is the considered view of the departments concerned that, even if such a person has in fact been guilty of a war crime committed abroad, it is unlikely, should he have acquired the status of a landed immigrant in Canada, that he could be punished in or deported from Canada for such activities. The Canadian Criminal Code does not extend to crimes committed outside this country-with one or two exceptions which are not relevant to the present circumstances- and, once an immigrant has acquired Canadian domicile, he is not subject to deportation for any but a specific and limited number of crimes which have been committed in this country and which are not relevant to the matter at issue.
I am sure the hon. member will recognize that there is a conflict in principle here between the grave concern we may have that persons who may have been guilty of the most abhorrent crimes have not been brought to justice and a basic principle which we have inherited from British justice, that criminal law should not be made retroactive in its application. However, with regard to the
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion policy of the Department of Manpower and Immigration concerning the admission of persons in respect of whom there might be evidence of this kind, in the future I am sure the Minister of Manpower and Immigration and his officials will take notice of this question and bear it particularly in mind with regard to future applications.

HEALTH AND WELFARE-PROTECTION OF NUTRITION STANDARDS FOLLOWING MILK PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two days ago, in view of the fact that the price of milk was to go up by two cents a quart within a month, I asked the Prime Minister what plans he and the government have to protect the nutrition standards of individuals and families on low incomes. Mr. Speaker said that that was a question which should not be asked at that time, on orders of the day. We have talked about reforms here in this house and I should very much like to see a change made in the rules so that it would be possible to ask such questions on the orders of the day, especially questions which have to do with nutrition, housing and other important problems which affect the consumers of the country.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
My question was based on two news stories, one of which appeared in a Toronto paper and the other in an Ottawa paper. The Toronto paper mentioned that a two cent increase in the price of milk is expected on May 1. The Ottawa paper mentioned two cents or three cents. When I investigated the story I was first inclined to think that what we had been told was correct, that this increase in the price of milk would help the farmer. However, I discovered that the director of the milk marketing board for Ontario clearly pointed out that in any case only one cent of the two cent increase woud go to the farmer, and if the story in the Ottawa newspaper is correct that three of the leading dairies here will increase the price of milk by three cents, the farmer will still get only one cent and the dairies will get the other two. He also stated that the one cent received by the farmer would be practically wiped out because of a decrease in the consumption of milk. As a result I am beginning to wonder whether this increase will go to the farmer or whether the dairies will cash in.
[Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) .1
April 13, 1967
I am concerned with the living standards of the people in this country on low incomes. According to Canada's food guide, a publication of our own Department of National Health and Welfare, children up to 11 years of age require 2J cups or 20 fluid ounces of milk per day, adolescents require 4 cups or 32 fluid ounces per day, adults require 1J cups or 12 fluid ounces per day, and expectant and nursing mothers require 4 cups or 32 fluid ounces per day.
Nutritional experts suggest that milk is essential for growing children, pregnant women and nursing mothers, and that there is no other food which will provide calcium in sufficient quantity. A child would have to consume 7J cups of raw cabbage in order to obtain the same amount of calcium obtained in one quart of milk. When considering that a child needs 2J cups of milk per day one realizes how ridiculous it would be to suggest that cabbage could be used as a substitute.
I am also informed that one would have to drink 11 cups of orange juice to get the same amount of calcium obtained in one quart of milk. Calcium is a basic need for healthy teeth and bones.
According to the best information I have available the consumption of milk has been dropping over the years. In 1940, Canadians consumed 1,160 pounds of fluid milk per year per person. By 1950 this consumption had dropped to 1,140, by 1960 to 900 pounds, and in 1965 the consumption was 907 pounds per person. There were increases and decreases in consumption in the intervening years, but the figures I have given indicate a definite trend.
I do not know all the reasons for this trend but the basic one is the increased cost of milk during the years. On January 31, 1940, whole milk cost 11 cents a quart here in Ottawa. By 1951 the price had increased to 22 cents a quart. Last year there were two increases in the price of milk, one in March and the second in July. Today the cost of a quart of whole milk in Ottawa is 30 cents.
These increases in costs are beginning to interfere with the nutritional standard of people in this country. I should like to know what is going to be done about this situation to assist those families on low income. These days we hear a great deal about physical fitness. A man who raises chickens once said that if a small chick's nutritional needs were neglected for even one day, the chick would

April 13, 1967	COMMONS
be unable to recover that loss during its entire life. If that is true for chicks, what about children?

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) and I appreciate her concern in this most important matter. I must hasten to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I prefer not to compare children with chickens. In my opinion children have a far higher priority. My interest is a very personal one because I have three children and I recognize the importance and need of nutrition and nutritional value for the children of today and for our future generations.
I am sure the hon. member is well aware of the fact that the government is as concerned as everybody else that Canadians have access to food of the highest nutritional quality. While I cannot with any great wisdom comment on a possible increase in the price of milk, I can assure the hon. member that the Department of National Health and Welfare is obliged to ensure that milk is clean and safe and meets adequate standards of nutrition and purity. One of the most economical and best sources of nutrient value in milk is in powdered milk, and as far as we know to date this commodity will not be affected by the price increase.
I should like also, if I may, to draw attention to a recent conference that I had the great privilege and pleasure of attending. I refer to the conference on child and maternal health. I think this government has made every effort to ensure that all Canadians, whatever their means, will be able to provide their families with sufficient quantities of milk.
I would refer particularly to the Canada Assistance Plan. This plan was enacted by parliament to ensure that people who do not have means adequate to provide food and other necessities can, through the assistance of the provincial and federal governments, meet the needs of their families for these necessities. I would like to assure the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway that not

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 12, 1967, I put the following question to the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote):
In view of the large number of representations received from the far-away county of Bonaventure and a few communities in the county of Gaspd because of the long delays in the local delivery of mail, could the minister investigate to see whether such a deplorable situation could be corrected, if he is anxious to achieve the intended purpose in implementing the mail delivery by truck?
In raising such a question, which I admit, Mr. Speaker, is not of national urgency, my intention was not to delay unduly the normal proceedings of this house nor to embarrass the minister, but rather to point out to him in a particular way a problem which, in the area concerned, is considered as one of great local urgency.
In order to show more clearly the seriousness of the problem, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be appropriate to give a brief historical account of the recent changes that occurred in the delivery of mail in the constituencies of Bonaventure and Gaspe.
For many years, numerous representations were made to the Post Office Department, through local parliament members, responsible bodies such as the district chamber of commerce, several local chambers of commerce, municipal councils, etc., in order to improve postal service on the southern shore of the Gaspe peninsula, from Cross Point, in the constituency of Bonaventure, up to Gaspe, in the county bearing the same name.
The Gaspe peninsula, which unfortunately is always considered as too remote every time one insists on establishing industries in that area which would improve its economy and even attract members of the professional classes, doctors, lawyers, to provide normal and essential services, has suffered and is still suffering from this remoteness, as regards mail delivery.
14912	COMMONS DEBATES	April 13, 1967
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
The present minister is well acquainted with the Gaspe peninsula; since his appointment to the department which he is now heading he has thoroughly visited the Gaspe area and obtained on the spot, not only from those who make use of the mail, but also from the post office employees and civic authorities some information in the light of which he has set himself to the task not to attain perfection in the mail distribution in the Gaspe peninsula, but at least to bring some considerable improvements.
For example, in order to dispatch the outgoing and incoming mail in the shortest possible time, the Post Office Department initiated on February 1 last on the southern coast of the Gaspe peninsula, the transport of mail by truck, forgoing the traditional mode of transport, the railway.
An experiment had been made last year whereby second class mail and newspapers were moved by truck; the experiment had proved most satisfactory to the whole population.
In spite of this, Mr. Speaker, the new system inaugurated on February 1 last does not seem to operate to the people's satisfaction. It must be said that the numerous storms that struck the Gaspe peninsula last winter did not help matters. Still, February, March and half of April have gone by and the situation has not improved. Delays do not seem frequent in the delivery of mail from Gaspe to outside points, such as Montreal, Quebec and Ottawa, for instance.
As proof of this, I have here a letter from the secretary and general manager of the Gaspe C.F.U., Mr. Jobin, to the Postmaster General. Dated April 10, mailed on April 10 at Black Cape, in the Gaspe peninsula, it reached the House of Commons on April 11.
In general, complaints deal with mail deliveries between local post offices. The trouble is with the routing of the mails between post offices in Gaspe.
In the same letter addressed to the Postmaster General by Mr. Jobin,-he mentions, for instance, a letter mailed on March 31, 1967, in New Richmond, in the riding of Bon-aventure, to the parish priest at Grande-Riviere, 85 miles away. It reached its destination on April 5. It took 6 days to cover 85 miles, whereas another letter from Gaspe took only one day to cover 700 miles.

Mr. Speaker, that is a new service and, as in the case of any new business, before the personnel is used to its operation and its organization in every detail, it may take some time, and some difficulties we are not accustomed to may arise.
Tonight, however, I would ask the hon. minister, whose efficiency is only equalled by his talents and stature and who, in establishing transportation by truck in Gaspd, wanted not to delay the delivery of mail but to improve it considerably, to insist that his officials keep their eye on the present situation in Gaspe, in the best interest of those who use the mails and of the Post Office Department in general.

maintopic: POSTAL SERVICE-REQUEST FOR IMPROVEMENT IN GASPE AND BONA VENTURE CONSTITUENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I readily understand that the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State (Mr. Bechard) is somewhat disappointed by the reorganization of postal services in the Gaspe peninsula.
If I were living there, I would possibly be disappointed also. But I should like it understood, Mr. Speaker, that we have undertaken a complete reorganization of mail delivery in the Gaspe peninsula. This reorganization is in two stages: the first, as the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Bechard) mentioned, was first to carry outside mail by truck instead of by railway. And the same thing applies to the mail from Gaspe to the outside.
The second stage is the reorganization of mail distribution within the Gaspe peninsula. This phase, not yet completed, produces some temporary delays in mail deliveries.
For instance, sorting which used to be done on the train between some centres of the Gaspe peninsula, is now done in the offices and the distributing offices which we organized.
We still have to organize the rural routes before June 1st, and many small post offices will also disappear because too much mail is now spread about in too many small post offices and the postmasters, even though they would like to complete the mail bags intended for a given place, must, to complete a bag, put in it several letters which are often sent to a community where the addressee does not live, and that causes undue delay.
But I can assure the hon. member that, before very long, instead of finding fault with the Post Office Department, he will only have congratulations to offer that department,

because we think that within a few months, the reorganization will be fully completed and the Gaspe peninsula will then enjoy one of the best mail services in Canada. That experiment which we tried this year in the Gaspe peninsula will surely be carried out elsewhere in the country.
